newsitem.title: JAPAN: Strict European budgets won't hurt recovery-Santer.
newsitem.headline: Strict European budgets won't hurt recovery-Santer.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer on Thursday dismissed worries that Europe's headlong drive to cut budget deficits ahead of the launch of its new single currency would drag down recovery.
"At this moment, we have signals that say for many countries, there is an economic recovery," Santer told Reuters in an interview.

"So I can see in our forecasts for 1997 that there could be an increase of GDP (gross domestic product) of about 2.4 percent. I think that is much better than we reached in...1996," said Santer, who is in Tokyo for a state visit following Monday's annual European Union-Japan summit.
The Commission is the executive of the European Union.
"We have to be aware that sound public finances are never in contradiction with good economic recovery in member states. The opposite is the reality in past years," Santer added.

Several European countries have recently announced plans to bring their 1997 budgets in line with the strict fiscal benchmarks laid out in the treaty on European unity forged in the Dutch city of Maastricht in 1992.

The International Monetary Fund said last month that European nations were generally expected to enjoy faster economic growth in 1997, but that many had tough economic problems. It said the forecasts could prove too rosy if the deficit-cutting drive dampened growth more than expected.
Analysts have said that in some cases the austere budgets contained creative accounting as well as one-off measures.
Santer, however, said he was "in general" satisfied with the willingness of EU member states to take steps to meet the strict fiscal criteria for joining the currency union.
"The single currency is on track, and is on the right track, and will be achieved in January 1999," he said.

Asked about French President Jacques Chirac's comments earlier this week casting doubt on Italy's chance of being in the first wave of countries joining Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), due to start on January 1, 1999, he said: "France and Italy are doing their homework and the results of their homework seems to me to be going in the right direction.

"So I can only encourage the governments like France, like Italy, like Spain, like Portugal, to maintain this political will and to maintain also the track they engage now for their own budgetary policies," he added.

Chirac's remarks drew a swift response from Italy, which accused him of meddling in Rome's affairs. But Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Wednesday that Chirac had told him the remarks were a "misunderstanding".

Asked about the likely impact on foreign exchange markets of the single European currency, the Euro, to be brought in by EMU, Santer said: "I think...that the single currency has to play a major role in the stabilisation of other currencies, especially between the dollar and the yen."
Santer, who met Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto later on Thursday, said economic issues remained on Europe's agenda with Japan, though ties now also encompass broad political matters.
"I would be very clear...we have economic and trade matters to discuss and they would remain on our agenda for the future, of course," he said.

Europe is keen to see Japan continue to deregulate its economy, a message Santer delivered to Japanese business groups over lunch. "We are satisfied by the last deregulation actions by Japan. Now we have to elevate that," he told Reuters.

Santer, due to leave Japan on Friday for Dublin for an informal chat with other EU leaders on a new treaty needed to handle an influx of new members from Eastern Europe and the Mediterranean, said he expected no decisions there.
But he added: "I hope from Dublin next weekend there would be a real political signal that our ambitions would be as high as possible."
